{{short description|Geometric operation on  convex polytopes}}
{{distinguish|enlargement (geometry)}}
[[Image:Expanding pentagon.png|thumb|An example of expanding [[pentagon]] into a [[decagon]] by moving edges away from the center and inserting new edges in the gaps. The ''expansion'' is ''uniform'' if all the edges are the same length.]]
[[File:P2-A5-P3.gif|thumb|Animation showing an expanded [[cube]] (and [[octahedron]])]]

In [[geometry]], '''expansion''' is a [[polytope]] operation where [[Facet (mathematics)|facets]] are separated and moved radially apart, and new facets are formed at separated elements ([[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]], [[Edge (geometry)|edges]], etc.). Equivalently this operation can be imagined by keeping facets in the same position but reducing their size.

The expansion of a [[Regular polytope|regular]] [[convex polytope]] creates a [[uniform polytope|uniform]] convex polytope.

For polyhedra, an expanded polyhedron has all the [[Face (geometry)|faces]] of the original polyhedron, all the faces of the [[dual polyhedron]], and new square faces in place of the original edges.

== Expansion of regular polytopes ==

According to [[Coxeter]], this multidimensional term was defined by [[Alicia Boole Stott]]<ref>Coxeter, ''Regular Polytopes'' (1973), p. 123. p.210</ref> for creating new polytopes, specifically starting from [[regular polytope]]s to construct new [[uniform polytope]]s.

The ''expansion'' operation is symmetric with respect to a regular polytope and its [[Dual polyhedron#Dual polytopes and tessellations|dual]]. The resulting figure contains the [[Facet (geometry)|facets]] of both the regular and its dual, along with various prismatic facets filling the gaps created between intermediate dimensional elements.

It has somewhat different meanings by [[dimension]].  In a [[Wythoff construction]], an expansion is generated by reflections from the first and last mirrors. In higher dimensions, lower dimensional expansions can be written with a subscript, so e<sub>2</sub> is the same as t<sub>0,2</sub> in any dimension.

By dimension:
* A regular {p} [[polygon]] expands into a regular 2n-gon. 
** The operation is identical to [[Truncation (geometry)|truncation]] for polygons, e{p} = e<sub>1</sub>{p} = t<sub>0,1</sub>{p} = t{p} and has [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]] {{CDD|node_1|p|node_1}}.
* A regular {p,q} [[polyhedron]] (3-polytope) expands into a polyhedron with [[vertex configuration]] ''p.4.q.4''.
**This operation for polyhedra is also called [[Cantellation (geometry)|cantellation]], e{p,q} = e<sub>2</sub>{p,q} = t<sub>0,2</sub>{p,q} = rr{p,q}, and has Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_1|p|node|q|node_1}}.
**: [[Image:Cube cantellation sequence.svg|480px]]
**: For example, a rhombicuboctahedron can be called an ''expanded cube'', ''expanded octahedron'', as well as a ''cantellated cube'' or ''cantellated octahedron''.
* A regular {p,q,r} [[4-polytope]] (4-polytope) expands into a new 4-polytope with the original {p,q} cells, new cells {r,q} in place of the old vertices, p-gonal prisms in place of the old faces, and r-gonal prisms in place of the old edges. 
** This operation for 4-polytopes is also called [[Runcination (geometry)|runcination]], e{p,q,r} = e<sub>3</sub>{p,q,r} = t<sub>0,3</sub>{p,q,r}, and has Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_1|p|node|q|node|r|node_1}}.
* Similarly a regular {p,q,r,s} [[5-polytope]] expands into a new 5-polytope with facets {p,q,r}, {s,r,q}, {p,q}×{ } [[Uniform_4-polytope#Prismatic_uniform_s|prism]]s, {s,r}×{ } prisms, and {p}''×''{s} [[duoprism]]s. 
** This operation is called [[sterication]], e{p,q,r,s} = e<sub>4</sub>{p,q,r,s} = t<sub>0,4</sub>{p,q,r,s} = 2r2r{p,q,r,s} and has Coxeter diagram {{CDD|node_1|p|node|q|node|r|node|s|node_1}}.

The general operator for expansion of a regular n-polytope is t<sub>0,n−1</sub>{p,q,r,...}. New regular <!--not necessarily [[simplex]]--> facets are added at each vertex, and new prismatic polytopes are added at each divided edge, face, ... [[Ridge (geometry)|ridge]], etc.
